source.title: On the Generalization Mystery in Deep Learning

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures per-example gradient coherence and reports how it changes between real and randomized datasets, then tests robust gradient aggregation as a way to alter memorization and generalization. These are conceptual tests of V1, using different measurements and interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests real-versus-randomized-label settings in Appendix E, but the supplied text gives those outcomes only in figures. Figure 1's detailed text result compares natural ImageNet images with Gaussian-noise images, not random labels, so it is recorded under fits_no_version. Cited findings from other studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: R1–R4 compare natural and fixed randomized labels using training and test accuracy under vanilla SGD without explicit regularization, directly testing V1 with the original type of method and measure. Gradient coherence is an additional measure, not itself a test of any listed version. The supplied text does not preserve readable accuracy curves sufficient for a complete V1 verdict.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors propose that coherent per-example gradients preserve algorithmic stability and explain generalization, support this account with real-versus-random experiments and robust-gradient interventions, and acknowledge that whole-network coherence can conceal layer differences. Their generalization bound is qualitative and extremely loose; these results do not establish a tight predictive guarantee.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses standard vanilla SGD without explicit regularization for its real-versus-randomized dataset measurements, and also proposes and evaluates winsorized or median gradient aggregation. The fully described main comparison randomizes input pixels rather than labels.
record.method_sensitivity: The coherence result varies by architecture and layer: AlexNet's whole-network coherence on Gaussian-noise inputs can peak at 40, while its first convolutional layer remains near the orthogonal limit. The authors also report that coherence evolves during training and differs between training and test samples.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet-50 fits both natural ImageNet and Gaussian-noise training images nearly perfectly, while only the natural-image condition shows non-trivial held-out generalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorization capacity for random inputs can coexist with generalization on natural inputs under the same architecture and SGD recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: During ResNet-50 training, natural-image gradient coherence corresponds to helping tens of sampled examples, compared with approximately one or two for Gaussian-noise images.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient coherence distinguishes natural-image generalization from random-input memorization in this ResNet-50 experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: AlexNet's whole-network coherence on Gaussian-noise inputs peaks at 40 despite near-orthogonal gradients in its first convolutional layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whole-network gradient coherence can conceal layers involved in memorization.

record.problems: The paper's random-label comparisons in Appendix E are figure-only in the supplied text, so their outcomes cannot be extracted reliably. The main text's detailed random-data comparison randomizes input pixels rather than labels. Coherence is acknowledged to be a blunt whole-network measure, and batch normalization requires an imputation method.
record.rows_left_out: The MNIST random-pixel and winsorization experiments, M3 experiments, easy/hard ImageNet comparisons, noisy-label coherence figures, and additional appendix runs were not extracted as separate rows because they do not provide textual outcomes for V1's exact random-label comparison or test another listed version. Random-label comparisons from Appendix E were kept as figure-only rows R1–R4.

untested.parts: The original small Inception and Inception V3 configurations are not tested. For the configurations actually tested, the complete held-out accuracy contrast is measured but unreadable in the supplied text.
No width sweep measuring test error beyond the width needed for interpolation; the proposed explanation of width benefits is future work.
No controlled convolutional-versus-fully-connected generalization comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
No adaptive-versus-SGD optimizer comparison; studying Adam is proposed as future work.
No fixed-epoch comparison of held-out performance across batch sizes. Discussion of batch-size effects relies on other studies.
No dropout intervention measuring held-out error.
No measurement of magnitude-aware sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps. Critiques of flatness as a universal explanation do not test this narrower correlational claim.
No removal and retraining comparison using examples ranked by label memorization influence.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V1. Appendix E's prose establishes qualitative random-label fitting evidence overlooked by the record, but does not establish all components of V1 without readable curves. Accordingly, no supports, limits_scope, or challenges label is justified from the supplied text alone. The none-linked rows retain valid findings; cannot_determine refers to their inability to establish a listed version, not uncertainty about those findings.

versions.untested_parts: The paper's randomized-label comparisons are shown only in figures, without textual outcome descriptions sufficient to determine their results. Its fully described ImageNet comparison uses Gaussian-noise inputs rather than random labels.
No width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
The paper measures gradient coherence, not magnitude-aware sharpness.

rows.subject: ResNet-50

rows.check: Gradient coherence measures a different construct from every listed version. The numerical interpretation includes the example itself; describing the count exclusively as other examples slightly overstates it.

rows.subject: AlexNet

rows.baseline: natural-image condition: peak is more than 2× the random-input peak
rows.note: The authors explicitly say the whole-network metric is a blunt instrument: the first convolutional layer on random data is near the orthogonal limit, while higher layers have comparable coherence.
rows.check: The peak coherence of 40 and the layer-dependent limitation are explicitly reported, but neither measures magnitude-aware sharpness or any other listed version. Replace the erroneous numbers_found entry with the actual reported peak.

relation.reason: The original-versus-randomized-label experiments directly test V1. The ImageNet experiments use ResNet-50 and AlexNet; none is an Inception V3 replication.

tranche.reason: The study compares original and randomized labels using vanilla SGD without explicit regularization and train/test accuracy, the same method and measure as the V1 original experiment.

source_check.notes: The recovered primary PDF is arXiv:2203.10036v3 by Satrajit Chatterjee and Piotr Zielinski, matching the extracted text. Figures 12–15 support qualitative outcomes; no curve values were digitized. Appendix E says settings were chosen for almost-perfect randomized-data training accuracy with no explicit regularizers; CIFAR-10 AlexNet inputs were resized to 224×224. No material first-check omission found.
